messages.author: 0325c6a976085eab
messages.subject: Re: model with formative and reflexive indicators
parts:
I don't know of any SEM software that can fit that model - it is not identified (without a lot of constraints).

If you think about this in path tracing terms, the effect from:

x1 to y3 = x1 -> y1 * y1 -> y3
x2 to y3 = x2 -> y1 * y1 -> y3
x3 to y3 = x3 -> y1 * y1 -> y3

The path from y1 -> y3 is not doing anything here - it's just a multiplier - it could double in value, and the formative effects from x1:x3 to y1 would halve, and the model would be identical.

To identify the model, first, remove the latent variables y1 and y2, and regression y3 directly on x1:x6.

It's still problematic - y4 only has one indicator. That has no error variance, and you need to constrain its loading to 1. But that means that it is equivalent to it being an indicator of y3. y4 isn't doing anything (except making your model more complex).

Jeremy

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: model with formative and reflexive indicators
parts:
Yes, using the Henseler-Ogasawara specification--see attached. With p indicators for a factor, you replace the p residual variances with p - 1 additional variables, so that the p observed variables are represented by p new variables, making the p new variables composites. In this way, you have complete freedom to represent any group of observed variables in a model by either a composite or a common factor. If you want some sample lavaan syntax, I demonstrated this in a presentation at the American Psych Association convention last summer. Slides and syntax are available at:
https://osf.io/ghxdu
--Ed Rigdon

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: model with formative and reflexive indicators
parts:
The github version of lavaan (0.6-20) has improved support for
composites. The goal is to allow for a seamless integration of both
latent variables and composites in the same model.

Try this toy example (after you have installed the github version):

library(lavaan)

# generate some data
pop.model <- '
eta1 <~ 1*x11 + 0.4*x12 + 0.6*x13
eta2 =~ 1*x21 + 0.8*x22 + 0.9*x23
eta3 <~ 1*x31 + 0.2*x32 + 0.5*x33 + 0.3*x34
eta4 =~ 1*x41 + 0.7*x42 + 0.8*x43

# indicators composites
x11 ~~ 6*x11
x12 ~~ 5*x12
x13 ~~ 2*x13

x31 ~~ 7*x31
x32 ~~ 3*x32
x33 ~~ 2*x33
x34 ~~ 5*x34

x11 ~~ 2*x12 + 1.2*x13
x12 ~~ 1.5*x13

x31 ~~ 0.9*x32
x31 ~~ 0.5*x33
x31 ~~ 1.2*x34
x32 ~~ 0.7*x33
x32 ~~ 1.8*x34
x33 ~~ 0.5*x34

# indicators latent variables
x21 ~~ 0.5*x21
x22 ~~ 0.5*x22
x23 ~~ 0.5*x23

x41 ~~ 0.5*x41
x42 ~~ 0.5*x42
x43 ~~ 0.5*x43

# latent variances
eta2 ~~ 1*eta2
eta4 ~~ 1*eta4

# structural part
eta3 ~ 0.5*eta1 + 0.6*eta2
eta4 ~ 0.1*eta1 + 0.3*eta3 + 0.2*eta2

eta1 ~~ 0.1*eta2
'
Data <- simulateData(pop.model, sample.nobs = 200L, empirical = TRUE)


# fit a model with both latent variables and composites
model <- '
eta1 <~ x11 + x12 + x13
eta2 =~ x21 + x22 + x23
eta3 <~ x31 + x32 + x33 + x34
eta4 =~ x41 + x42 + x43

# structural part
eta3 ~ eta1 + eta2
eta4 ~ eta1 + eta2 + eta3
'

fit <- sem(model, data = Data, verbose = TRUE,
optim.gradient = "numerical")
summary(fit)


Note the use of optim.gradient = "numerical" when calling the sem()
function! That is because I have not derived the analytic gradient yet
for this setting.

A paper about the underlying methodology is under preparation.

Yves.
